newsitem.title: UK: Foreign investors bemoan heavy taxation in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investors bemoan heavy taxation in Russia.

text.p: Russia's complex tax system was strangling profits and limiting progress and should be overhauled, foreign companies with operations in Russia said on Wednesday.
"We wish we could start making profit, just for a change," Mars Inc Moscow representative Alexander Chalnev told an investment conference in London.
"(Russia has) a very imperfect taxation system, we pay 18 different taxes, including those which are unheard of in the West, like tax on advertising and other business expenses," Chalnev said.
On Tuesday European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) president Jacques de Larosiere listed the former Soviet bloc's taxation system as a major obstacle deterring foreign investors.
Chalnev said Mars paid about $60 million in taxes in 1996.

"Let me be blunt," he said: "We had to put on hold some of our projects for Russia, we do not progress as rapidly as we could precisely because we are not sure where we will end up financially, economically and fiscally," he said.
Chalnev said despite this, Mars had faith that Russia would overcome its difficulties "much sooner than the rest of the world could expect".
"If we were interested just in the money for ourselves, we probably would have never come to Russia: too many uncertainties, too much hassle," he said.
He said the company hoped to gain from President Boris Yeltsin's recent "Buy Russian" campaign, as Mars manufactured locally.
"Is Russian chocolate worse than imported chocolate? No, it's better," Yeltsin said in a nationwide radio address on Tuesday.
Ross Stobie, general manager of British Gas Moscow, which has a 50 percent shareholding in Komi Arctic Oil (KAO), said they had paid millions in taxes.
"There is a myriad of regulations and procedures and we really hope for simplification (of the system) to reduce the overall tax burden."
Stobie also called for fresh incentives for further foreign investment.
"We have no fears of investing in Russia, we are looking to expand, however we do need the help of the local authorities," he said.
Jack Meiland, managing director of the STC Group, a Scottish/Russian entity, told investors they had to have an open mind and be flexible in dealing with Russia.
But he said he was optimistic about the future and further plans for expansion. He said linking up with "reliable Russian partners" was of key importance.
Telenor Invest AS representative from St Petersburg Goran Olson agreed: "Choice of (business) partners is crucial."
Olson said patience was required when introducing market economy principles to Russia.
"The further from Moscow and St Petersburg you go, the more patience you need," he said.
